rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doomsday proclamation is so overwhelming that it deafens people to worldly sounds and makes them hear the affairs of the next life.
rows.anchor: إن صيحة القيامة مسمعة تصم عن الدنيا وتسمع أمور الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fleeing clause replaces the preceding time clause; its omitted consequence is that each person is occupied with himself, as the next verse indicates.
rows.anchor: يوم يفر: بدل من إذا، وجواب إذا محذوف تقديره: اشتغل كل إنسان بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The terror explains the flight: even the messengers cry, “Myself, myself.”
rows.anchor: من قول الرسل: «نفسي نفسي»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is fear of relatives' claims, since close ties invite demands for rights: siblings reproach, parents accuse, spouses and children blame.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خوف التبعات، لأن الملابسة تقتضي المطالبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers understand yughni as making a person independent of concern for others; al-Zuhri and several named readers read yaʿni, meaning the matter concerns him.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يغنيه: أي عن النظر في شأن الآخر من الإغناء

rows.speaker: الزهري وابن محيصن وابن أبي عبلة وحميد وابن السميفع
rows.claim: These readers have يعنيه, from ʿanānī al-amr: the matter concerned or targeted me.
rows.anchor: والزهري وابن محيصن وابن أبي عبلة وحميد وابن السميفع: يعنيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Musfira means radiant, from the dawn becoming bright; tarhaquha means covers it, and qatarah is dust.
rows.anchor: مسفرة: مضيئة، من أسفر الصبح: أضاء، وترهقها: تغشاها، قترة: أي غبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One distinction makes ghubrah the gloom of a worried frown and qatarah earthly dust; another makes ghubrah earth-soil and qatarah smoke-like blackness.
rows.anchor: والأولى ما يغشاه من العبوس عند الهم، والثانية من غبار الأرض

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says ghubrah is what descends to earth, while qatarah rises toward the sky.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم: الغبرة: ما انحطت إلى الأرض، والقترة: ما ارتفعت إلى السماء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce qatarah with an open tā; Ibn Abi ʿAbla uses a vowelless tā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: قترة، بفتح التاء وابن أبي عبلة: بإسكانها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inkadarat means the stars scattered; Abu ʿUbayda glosses it as falling down like vessels when broken, and al-ʿAjjaj supplies poetic usage.
rows.anchor: انكدرت النجوم: انتثرت. وقال أبو عبيدة: انصبت كما تنصب القعاب إذا كسرت

rows.speaker: العجاج
rows.claim: Al-ʿAjjaj's line describes a falcon swooping down and witnesses the sense of falling or scattering in inkadara.
rows.anchor: قال العجاج يصف صقرا: أبصر حرمات فلاة فانكدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIshar is the plural of ʿushara, a she-camel ten months into pregnancy, a name retained until she gives birth at the year's end.
rows.anchor: العشار جمع عشراء، وهي الناقة التي مر لحملها عشرة أشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʿṭil means emptying something or leaving it neglected.
rows.anchor: التعطيل: التفريغ والإهمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-wahsh denotes land animals whose nature is not to become sociable with human beings.
rows.anchor: الوحش: حيوان البر الذي ليس في طبعه التآنس ببني آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mawʾudah is a girl buried alive; the term is linked to being moved under earth until death, and to ittaʾid, meaning proceed ponderously.
rows.anchor: الموءودة: البنت التي تدفن حية، وأصله من النقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kashṭ means peeling, as in stripping a sheep's hide.
rows.anchor: الكشط: التقشير، كشطت جلد الشاة: سلخته عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-khunnas are hidden or withdrawing bodies; khunūs denotes contraction and concealment, as in withdrawing among people.
rows.anchor: الخنس جمع خانس، والخنوس: الانقباض والاستخفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-kunnas are those entering a kanas, the shelter where gazelles retreat.
rows.anchor: الكنس جمع كانس وكانسة، يقال: كنس إذا دخل الكناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same word khunnas can describe a nose whose tip recedes slightly behind the lip.
rows.anchor: والخنس: تأخر الأنف عن الشفة مع ارتفاع قليل من الأرنبة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says ʿasʿasa describes night when only a little of it remains.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: عسعس الليل وعسس، إذا لم يبق منه إلا القليل

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil says ʿasʿasa can mean that night either approaches or departs.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل: عسعس الليل: أقبل وأدبر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad classifies ʿasʿasa as a word with opposite meanings.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: هو من الأضداد. وقال علقمة بن قرط:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the stars fell; he also says they changed and lost their light as they left their positions, like murky water.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس: تساقطت وعنه أيضا: تغيرت فلم يبق لها ضوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains are moved from the earth's surface or carried through the air like clouds; this occurs before pulverization, at the first terror of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وتسيير الجبال: أي عن وجه الأرض، أو سيرت في الجو تسيير السحاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camels are the Arabs' most prized wealth; neglect may mean leaving them unattended, ceasing milking, or not breeding them because people are occupied with themselves.
rows.anchor: والعشار: أنفس ما عند العرب من المال، وتعطيلها: تركها مسيبة مهملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them ʿishar names them by their former state; al-Qurṭubi says the image is hypothetical because no pregnant camels will remain at Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وأطلق عليها عشارا باعتبار ما سبق لها ذلك. قال القرطبي: وهذا على وجه المثل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says that people emerging from graves see their former prized camels among the gathered animals but ignore them, preoccupied with themselves.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إذا قاموا من القبور شاهدوا الوحوش والدواب محشورة وعشارهم فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations take ʿishar as clouds deprived of rain, abandoned homes, or fields whose crops are not cultivated.
rows.anchor: وقيل: العشار: السحاب، وتعطيلها من الماء فلا تمطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use emphatic ʿuṭṭilat; a light form is attributed to Mudar readers and, in al-Lawamiʿ, Ibn Kathir, though that book calls the latter attribution an error.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: عطلت بتشديد الطاء ومضر عن اليزيدي: بتخفيفها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥushirat means gathered from every direction.
rows.anchor: حشرت: أي جمعت من كل ناحية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says animals are gathered at death and neither raised nor present at Judgment; another report from him and Qatada and others includes every creature, even flies.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: جمعت بالموت، فلا تبعث ولا يحضر في القيامة غير الثقلين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbas says beasts are gathered to settle claims against one another, even the hornless animal's claim against the horned, then are told to die.
rows.anchor: وعنه: تحشر الوحوش حتى يقتص من بعضها لبعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An opinion says animals become dust after their disputes, except beautiful creatures that delight people, such as the peacock.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إذا قضي بينها ردت ترابا فلا يبقى منها إلا ما فيه سرور لبني آدم

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy says that during the first terror in this world, wild creatures flee across the earth and gather near humans for company.
rows.anchor: وقال أبي: في الدنيا في أول الهول تفر في الأرض وتجتمع إلى بني آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce ḥushirat with a light shin; al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn Maymun double it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: حشرت بخف الشين والحسن وعمرو بن ميمون: بشدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word sajjirat has been explained earlier in Surat al-Tur; in Khathʿam usage it means gathered.
rows.anchor: سجرت: جمعت، بلغة خثعم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya suggests the seas may be restrained and their turbulence contained so the terror does not make them overrun the land, deriving the word from a dog's collar.
rows.anchor: وقال هنا ابن عطية: ويحتمل أن يكون المعنى: ملكت وقيد اضطرابها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read sajjarat with a light jim, while the other canonical readers double it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو: بخف الجيم وباقي السبعة: بشدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce al-mawʾudah with hamza between the two waws as a passive participle; al-Bazzi has a variant with a hamza over a damma-vowelled waw, explained through vowel transfer or an alternate derivation from āda.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: الموؤدة، بهمزة بين الواوين، اسم مفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading has a damma on the first waw and softens the hamza by deleting it and moving its vowel; al-Aʿmash reads al-mawaddah with a still waw.
rows.anchor: وقرىء الموودة، بضم الواو الأولى وتسهيل الهمزة

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Hamza pauses on the form matching the written rasm; the readers treat that orthography as normative and binding.
rows.anchor: ونقل القراء أن حمزة يقف عليها كالموودة لأجل الخط لأنها رسمت كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read both verbs passively; asking the buried girl is a rebuke of those who buried girls, since the question ultimately addresses the perpetrators.
rows.anchor: وهذا السؤال هو لتوبيخ الفاعلين للوأد، لأن سؤالها يؤول إلى سؤال الفاعلين

rows.speaker: الحسن والأعرج
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Aʿraj read suʾilat with a kasra on the sin, following a dialect that says sāla without hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والأعرج: سئلت، بكسر السين، وذلك على لغة من قال

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar doubles the yāʾ because al-mawʾudah is a collective noun and the many individuals suit an intensive plural reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر: بشد الياء، لأن الموؤدة اسم جنس

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وعلي وابن عباس وجابر بن زيد وأبو الضحى ومجاهد
rows.claim: These authorities read the girl as the active subject of both verbs, voicing her question about the sin for which she was killed.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود وعلي وابن عباس وجابر بن زيد وأبو الضحى ومجاهد: سألت

rows.speaker: أبي وابن مسعود والربيع بن خثيم وابن يعمر
rows.claim: Ubayy, Ibn Masʿud, al-Rabiʿ ibn Khaytham, and Ibn Yaʿmar are also reported with an active “she asked” but passive “she was killed”; direct speech would use a second-person ending.
rows.anchor: بأي ذنب قتلت: مبنيا للمفعول بتاء التأنيث فيهما إخبارا عنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author describes the practice: a kept daughter might herd livestock until age six, then be dressed and led to a prepared pit, pushed in, and buried.
rows.anchor: وكان العرب إذا ولد لأحدهم بنت واستحياها، ألبسها جبة من صوف أو شعر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the stars withdraw by day and hide by night, then emerge from their places like wild animals leaving dens.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أي تخنس بالنهار وتكنس بالليل، أي تطلع في أماكنها

rows.speaker: عبد الله والنخعي وجابر بن زيد وجماعة
rows.claim: These authorities identify the hidden, moving objects as wild cattle, which perform these actions in their lairs.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله والنخعي وجابر بن زيد وجماعة: المراد بالخنس الجوار الكنس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak identify them as gazelles and explain khunnas as a descriptor also applied to bustards and wild cattle.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وابن جبير والضحاك: هي الظباء، والخنس من صفة الأنوق

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan takes ʿasʿasa as nightfall; its pairing with dawn, which breathes, supports two contrasting states.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: أقبل ظلامه، ويرجحه مقابلته بقوله

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says the oath covers night in both its arrival and departure; dawn is described as breathing because it brings breeze and spirit, metaphorically.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: أقسم بإقباله وإدباره وتنفسه كونه يجيء معه روح ونسيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sworn statement is that the Qurʾan is the speech of a noble messenger; the majority identify him as Gabriel, while another view identifies Muhammad.
rows.anchor: إنه: أي إن هذا المقسم عليه، أي إن القرآن لقول رسول كريم الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Karim denies every reproach and affirms all fitting praiseworthy qualities.
rows.anchor: وكريم صفة تقتضي نفي المذام كلها وإثبات صفات المدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description “possessor of strength” echoes the wording of 53:5.
rows.anchor: ذي قوة: كقوله: شديد القوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makin denotes the rank and standing fitting his proximity to the Throne; the Throne may also syntactically attach to makin, and he is obeyed among the close angels.
rows.anchor: عند ذي: الكينونة اللائقة من شرف المنزلة وعظم المكانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar and several readers pronounce thumma with a damma as a conjunction; most use the spatial adverb thamma. Al-Zamakhshari's reading with damma magnifies trustworthiness as Gabriel's best trait.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وأبو حيوة وأبو البرهسم وابن مقسم: ثم، بضم الثاء

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: Al-Lawamiʿ explains the conjunction as equivalent to “and”: Gabriel held both traits simultaneously; a temporal order would require transmitted evidence.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب اللوامح: بمعنى مطاع وأمين، وإنما صارت ثم بمعنى الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amin means credible and accepted in speech, entrusted with revelation and obedience to divine commands.
rows.anchor: أمين: مقبول القول يصدق فيما يقوله، مؤتمن على ما يرسل به من وحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage denies the accusations of madness that people made against Muhammad.
rows.anchor: نفى عنه ما كانوا ينسبونه إليه ويبهتونه به من الجنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kadhḥ is exertion that marks the self, from the verb for scratching skin; Ibn Muqbil and another poet illustrate the usage.
rows.anchor: الكدح: جهد النفس في العمل حتى يؤثر فيها، من كدح جلده إذا خدشه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥāra means returned; a poet compares a person to a meteor that returns to ash after shining.
rows.anchor: حار: رجع، قال الشاعر: وما المرء إلا كالشهاب وضوئه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shafaq is the redness after sunset when the time of the final evening prayer arrives; its root is linked to thinness and tenderness.
rows.anchor: الشفق: الحمرة بعد مغيب الشمس حين تأتي صلاة العشاء الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A derivation connects shafaq with something too thin to hold together, and with compassion because the heart softens; a poem uses the word in that sense.
rows.anchor: قيل: أصله من رقة الشيء، يقال شيء شفق: أي لا يتماسك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wasaq means gathered and joined; a wasq is sixty measures, and the word also describes collected food and gathered camels.
rows.anchor: وسق: ضم وجمع، ومنه الوسق: الأصواع المجموعة، وهي ستون صاعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says the moon's ittisaq is its fullness and evenness on the nights of the full moon, derived from gathering; muttasiq also means orderly.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: اتساق القمر: امتلاؤه واستواؤه ليالي البدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq describes one state following another; ṭabaq means something that matches or covers another.
rows.anchor: طبقا عن طبق: حال بعد حال، والطبق: ما طابق غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The matching layers of earth and a cover are called ṭabaq; al-Aʿraj ibn Habis and Imruʾ al-Qays illustrate successive states and rain blanketing the ground.
rows.anchor: إني امرؤ قد حلبت الدهر أشطره ... وساقني طبق منه إلى طبق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is Meccan and its connection with the preceding surah is clear.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية، واتصالها بما قبلها ظاهر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Farraʾ, and al-Zajjaj explain the sky's splitting as opening with clouds; another view makes it split from the terror of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: انشقت تنشق: أي تتصدع بالغمام، وقاله الفراء والزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers keep the feminine tāʾ vowelless in connection and pause; Ubayd ibn ʿAqil from Abu ʿAmr gives it a slight kasra at pause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بسكون تاء انشقت وما بعدها وصلا ووقفا

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: Al-Lawamiʿ treats the pausal kasra as a rhyme-like ending that clarifies tāʾ as a feminine verb marker rather than a noun ending; it is a Tayy dialect.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب اللوامح: فهذا من التغييرات التي تلحق الروي في القوافي

rows.speaker: ابن عطية وأبو حاتم
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes a slight pausal kasra to Abu ʿAmr, and Abu Hatim heard eloquent Qays speakers use the dialect.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية، وقرأ أبو عمرو: انشقت، يقف على التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse endings can be paused like rhymes, as in al-Ahzab; a Kuthayyir ʿAzza poem supplies an example.
rows.anchor: وإجراء الفواصل في الوقف مجرى القوافي مهيع معروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḏinat means listening to its Lord's command; a hadith about God listening to a prophet reciting beautifully illustrates the verb.
rows.anchor: وأذنت: أي استمعت وسمعت أمره ونهيه، وفي الحديث: «ما أذن الله بشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets use adhina for hearing: one contrasts deafness to praise with attention to insult; Qaʿnab and al-Hajjaf ibn Hakim also attest the usage.
rows.anchor: صم إذا سمعوا خيرا ذكرت به ... وإن ذكرت بسوء عندهم أذنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's listening is its obedience to God when He wills it to split, like the heavens' declaration that they came obediently.
rows.anchor: وإذنها: انقيادها لله تعالى حين أراد انشقاقها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن جبير
rows.claim: They say the sky rightly listened to God; al-Dahhak says it obeyed and rightly did so, and Qatada says it rightly performed the act.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن جبير: وحق لها أن تسمع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive wording has God as agent: He rightly imposed listening on the sky, since nothing in its substance prevents His power from splitting and dissolving it.
rows.anchor: وهذا الفعل مبني للمفعول، والفاعل هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan objects that al-Zamakhshari's phrase “the Omnipotent in His essence” insinuates Muʿtazili doctrine.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله القادر الذات دسيسة الاعتزال، وما أولع هذا الرجل بمذهب الاعتزال

rows.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك
rows.claim: Mujahid says the earth is leveled; al-Dahhak says its mountains are crushed as it is spread flat.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: سويت. وقال الضحاك: بسطت باندكاك جبالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith compares the earth's stretching to tanned leather from ʿUkaz, leaving each person only a footprint's space; the result is a smooth plain.
rows.anchor: ومنه الحديث: تمد الأرض مد الأديم العكاظي حتى لا يكون لبشر من الناس

rows.speaker: ابن جبير والجمهور
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr and most exegetes say the earth casts out its dead and empties itself of the living on its surface.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جبير والجمهور: ألقت ما في بطنها من الأموات، وتخلت ممن على ظهرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says it empties itself of mountains and seas; al-Zajjaj says treasures, but Abu Hayyan rejects this because treasures emerge at the Dajjal's appearance whereas the earth casts out the dead at Judgment.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: ومن الكنوز، وضعف هذا بأن ذلك يكون وقت خروج الدجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takhallat means the earth clings to nothing that had been inside it; its form conveys exerting the utmost effort to empty itself, figuratively, since God actually expels those things.
rows.anchor: وتخلت: أي عن ما كان فيها، لم تتمسك منهم بشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apodosis of idha may be borrowed from Surat al-Takwir or al-Infitar, or supplied by the statement that every person meets his toil; al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad take “you will meet it” as the answer.
rows.anchor: وجواب إذا محذوف، فإما أن يقدره الذي خرج به في سورة التكوير أو الانفطار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other parses make “O human” the answer with an omitted fa, add the waw before the earth clause, or make the first idha a subject with the second clause as predicate.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يا أيها الإنسان، على حذف الفاء تقديره: يا أيها الإنسان

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites grammarians who make inshaqqat the governing word for idha, though many reject this because idha is annexed to that verb.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وقال بعض النحويين: العامل انشقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan adopts the parse in which the time of the sky's splitting is the time of the earth's stretching; another view treats idha as an object of “remember,” not a conditional.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول نحن نختاره، وقد استدللنا على صحته فيما كتبناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth obeys its Lord by casting out what is in its belly and emptying itself.
rows.anchor: وأذنت لربها: أي في إلقاء ما في بطنها وتخليها

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says “the human” is al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, who argued with his brother Abu Salama about resurrection; the generic wording still includes everyone.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: المراد به الأسود بن عبد الأسد بن هلال المخزومي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another identification is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who labored for worldly gain, harmed the Messenger, and persisted in disbelief.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد أبي بن خلف، كان يكدح في طلب الدنيا وإيذاء الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the remote view that the address singles out the Prophet's toil in conveying revelation and enduring harm, rewarded at his meeting with God.
rows.anchor: وأبعد من ذهب إلى أنه الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم، والمعنى: إنك تكدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥijr means intellect; al-Farraʾ says a person of ḥijr restrains and protects himself, as though he were enclosed from harm.
rows.anchor: الحجر: العقل، قال الفراء: العرب تقول: إنه لذو حجر إذا كان قاهرا لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iram may be an ancient nation, the ancestor of all ʿAd, or a city; Zuhayr and al-Ruqayyat refer to Iram in verse.
rows.anchor: إرم: أمة قديمة، وقيل: اسم أبي عاد كلها، وهو عاد بن عوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jaba means to pierce, hew, or traverse a land; a poem illustrates crossing a country.
rows.anchor: جاب: خرق وقطع، تقول جبت البلاد أجوبها، إذا قطعتها وجاوزتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawṭ is the familiar whip; some linguists derive it from mixing, as in mixing blood, and al-Layth uses the verb for striking with a whip.
rows.anchor: السوط: آلة للضرب معروفة. قال بعض اللغويين: وهو مصدر من ساط يسوط

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd says suwīṭah describes property mixed together among people; Abu ʿUbayda explains lamma as eating everything on a tray.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو زيد: يقال أموالهم سويطة بينهم: أي مختلطة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda says lamma is consuming all the food on a tray; al-Hutayʾa and al-Nabigha provide poetic evidence for consuming and gathering, and jamm means great.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: لممت ما على الخوان، إذا أكلت جميع ما عليه بأسره.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most authorities classify the surah as Meccan; ʿAli ibn Abi Talha says it is Medinan.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية في قول الجمهور. وقال علي بن أبي طلحة: مدنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah follows the prior account of humbled and flourishing faces by describing arrogant disbelieving peoples and the contented soul; it answers turning away and disbelief with a threat that God is watching.
rows.anchor: ذكر الطوائف المتكبرين المكذبين المتجبرين الذين وجوههم خاشعة

rows.speaker: أبو الدينار الأعرابي
rows.claim: Abu al-Dinar al-Aʿrabi adds tanwin to al-fajr, al-watr, and yasr; Ibn Khalawayh compares the usage with Arabs' pausal tanwin at rhyme endings, even on verbs or definite forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو الدينار الأعرابي: والفجر، والوتر، ويسر بالتنوين في الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem illustrates tanwin-like endings in open rhymes; grammarians discuss this in unrestricted rhymes and in ordinary pausal speech.
rows.anchor: وهذا ذكره النحويون في القوافي المطلقة إذا لم يترنم الشاعر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Most read layālin ʿashr with tanwin; Ibn ʿAbbas has an annexed form, glossed as the nights of ten days after eliding the counted noun.
rows.anchor: وابن عباس: بالإضافة، فضبطه بعضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read al-watr with a fatḥa on waw and still tāʾ, a Quraysh dialect; several authorities use kasra on waw, a Tamim dialect, and further variants are transmitted.
rows.anchor: والجمهور: والوتر بفتح الواو وسكون التاء، وهي لغة قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most delete the yāʾ in yasr both connected and paused; Ibn Kathir retains it in both, while Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmr retain it only in connection.
rows.anchor: والجمهور: يسر بحذف الياء وصلا ووقفا وابن كثير: بإثباتها فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fajr most naturally means dawn in general, not one specified day; other reports identify it with the Day of Sacrifice, Friday, Dhul-Hijjah, the night at Jamʿ, or the first day of Muharram.
rows.anchor: أقسم به كما أقسم بالصبح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas also explains al-fajr as the whole day, the dawn prayer and its recitation, or the dawn of springs in rock.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا: الفجر: النهار كله

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير والكلبي وقتادة ومجاهد والضحاك والسدي وعطية العوفي
rows.claim: These authorities identify the ten nights as the first ten of Dhul-Hijjah; Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak also report the last ten nights of Ramadan.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الزبير والكلبي وقتادة ومجاهد والضحاك والسدي وعطية العوفي: هي عشر ذي الحجة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج ويمان ومسروق ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj specifies the first ten days; Yaman and others say the first ten of Muharram including Ashura; Masruq and Mujahid identify Moses' ten days.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: الأول منه ويمان وجماعة: الأول من المحرم ومنه يوم عاشوراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says Ibn ʿAbbas' view is strongest because of a rigorously authenticated hadith agreed upon by both canonical collections.
rows.anchor: قيل: والأظهر قول ابن عباس للحديث المتفق على صحته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night is sworn by as a kind, and yasr means it passes and disappears, as in the wording “when it departs.”
rows.anchor: والليل إذا يسر: قسم بجنس الليل، ويسري: يذهب وينقرض

rows.speaker: الأخفش وابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba instead take yasr as night moving within itself, like the expression “your night is asleep.”
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش وابن قتيبة: يسري فيه، فيكون من باب ليلك نائم

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي
rows.claim: Mujahid, ʿIkrima, and al-Kalbi identify the night as the night at Jamʿ, when people travel through it.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي: المراد ليلة جمع لأنه يسري فيها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري وابن الأنباري
rows.claim: The oath's answer is omitted: al-Zamakhshari supplies “We shall punish,” and Ibn al-Anbari supplies “Your Lord is watching.”
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وهو لنعذبن، يدل عليه قوله: ألم تر إلى قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers an omitted answer inferred from the end of the prior surah: people return to God and their reckoning is His responsibility.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن الجواب محذوف يدل عليه ما قبله من آخر سورة الغاشية

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil treats hal as equivalent to “indeed,” but Abu Hayyan objects that this leaves the oath without a sworn assertion; the question instead asks whether a rational person has enough evidence to take heed.
rows.anchor: وقول مقاتل: هل هنا في موضع تقديره: إن في ذلك قسما لذي حجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destroyed peoples are presented as a warning to Quraysh and an example of the fate of disbelieving nations.
rows.anchor: ثم وقف المخاطب على مصارع الأمم الكافرة الماضية مقصودا بذلك توعد قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAd may denote the descendants of ʿAwd, with early generations called first ʿAd and Iram after their grandfather and later ones the latter ʿAd; Mujahid and Qatada say Iram is a tribe, while Ibn Ishaq calls it the father of all ʿAd.
rows.anchor: وعاد هو عاد بن عوص، وأطلق ذلك على عقبه، ثم قيل للأولين منهم عادا الأولى

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most authorities identify Iram as a great city in Yemen; Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says Alexandria, Ibn al-Musayyib and al-Maqburi say Damascus, and Mujahid also glosses the word as ancient.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور: إرم مدينة لهم عظيمة كانت على وجه الدهر باليمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ in case and declension of ʿAd and Iram; most make Iram a diptote explanatory apposition or substitute, while variants connect it by annexation or vary its vowels.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بعاد مصر، وفا إرم بكسر الهمزة وفتح الراء والميم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak read Arim as a past verb meaning to decay or be ruined; the interpretation continues with the syntax of ḏāt.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس والضحاك: أرم فعلا ماضيا، أي بلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading with ḏāt in the accusative treats it as an object; ḏāt with kasra can describe a tribe or city, though the city fits “none like it in the lands” better.
rows.anchor: ذات بالكسر صفة لإرم وسواء كانت اسم قبيلة أو مدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant annexes Iram to ḏāt, with iram meaning a monument; the verb reading can mean God made the city rubble.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: إرم ذات، بإضافة إرم إلى ذات، والإرم: العلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: If ḏāt al-ʿimād describes the tribe, Ibn ʿAbbas takes it as their great height, likening their bodies to pillars.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: هي كناية عن طول أبدانهم، ومنه قيل: رفيع العماد

rows.speaker: عكرمة ومقاتل
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and Muqatil say the pillars are tent poles of a people who lived in tents; Ibn Zayd instead means their building pillars.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة ومقاتل: أعمدة بيوتهم التي كانوا يرحلون بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the phrase describes a city, its pillars are the stone supports of its buildings; it can also mean tall palaces or towers.
rows.anchor: وإذا كانت صفة للمدينة، فأعمدة الحجارة التي بنيت بها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid is also reported to take Iram as a verbal noun for perishing, meaning destruction like that of the people of the pillars; Abu Hayyan calls this strange.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن مجاهد: أرم مصدر، أرم يأرم إذا هلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes tell that Shaddad built an extraordinary city after hearing descriptions of Paradise, but a cry destroyed him and his people before he entered it.
rows.anchor: وذكر المفسرون أن ذات العماد مدينة ابتناها شداد بن عاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read lam yukhlaq passively, with mithl raised; Ibn al-Zubayr reads it actively with mithl as object and also has nun yakhluq. The pronoun can refer to the city or the tribe's strength.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: لم يخلق مبنيا للمفعول، مثلها رفع وابن الزبير: مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Wathab reads Thamud with tanwin, unlike the majority; jaba means they hewed the rock to make houses, as in 7:74.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب وثمود بالتنوين. والجمهور: بمنع الصرف. جابوا الصخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says Thamud first hewed mountains, rock, and marble and built 1,700 stone cities in Wadi al-Qura; another says they cut their valley or brought water through cleft stone.
rows.anchor: أول من نحت الجبال والصخور والرخام ثمود، وبنوا ألفا وسبعمائة مدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-awtad has been discussed in Surat Sad.
rows.anchor: ذي الأوتاد: تقدم الكلام على ذلك في سورة ص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ladhina can modify ʿAd, Thamud, and Pharaoh, stand as an object of blame, or be nominative after an omitted pronoun.
rows.anchor: الذين صفة لعاد وثمود وفرعون، أو منصوب على الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brief mention of punishment is expanded in Surat al-Haqqa; “pouring” conveys how swiftly it falls on its victims.
rows.anchor: فصب عليهم ربك سوط عذاب: أبهم هنا وأوضح في الحاقة وفي غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawṭ is a metaphor for recurring blows, unlike a sword; a poet compares the punishment to showers of blows.
rows.anchor: وخص السوط فاستعير للعذاب، لأنه يقتضي من التكرار والترداد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the worldly punishment is like a whip compared with what is prepared in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وذكر السوط إشارة إلى أن ما أحله بهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mirṣād is a place where watch is kept; it depicts God waiting to punish sinners so they cannot escape.
rows.anchor: والمرصاد والمرصد: المكان الذي يترتب فيه الرصد

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya proposes an intensified active participle meaning “the watcher”; Abu Hayyan rejects it because the preposition bāʾ cannot grammatically enter there.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ويحتمل أن يكون المرصاد في الآية اسم فاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rebukes Quraysh for treating wealth and children as signs of divine honor and their absence as humiliation; human is generic and the error occurs among Muslims too.
rows.anchor: ذكر تعالى ما كانت قريش تقوله وتستدل به على إكرام الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari links this to God's watch over sinners: God wants obedience and afterlife concern, while people seek immediate pleasure; Abu Hayyan flags the explicit Muʿtazili claim about divine will.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: بم اتصل قوله: فأما الإنسان؟ قلت: بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being tried by wealth tests gratitude, while restriction tests patience; both are forms of trial, as 21:35 says.
rows.anchor: لقوله تعالى: ونبلوكم بالشر والخير فتنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not call reduced provision humiliation: many righteous people, including Abu Sulayman Dawud al-Isfahani, lived with little.
rows.anchor: ولم يقابل فأكرمه بلفظ فأهانه، لأنه ليس من يضيق عليه الرزق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person who says “my Lord honored me” claims he deserves that honor; saying “He humiliated me” mistakes the absence of extra favor for humiliation.
rows.anchor: فلأنه إخبار منه على أنه يستحق الكرامة ويستوجبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ on the yāʾ in akramanī and ahānanī: Ibn Kathir retains both, Nafiʿ retains them in connection only, Abu ʿAmr allows either, and other canonical readers delete them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير: أكرمني وأهانني بالياء فيهما ونافع: بالياء وصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read fa-qadara with a light dāl; several others double it. The forms mean restriction, with doubling for emphasis rather than transitivity.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فقدر بخف الدال وأبو جعفر وعيسى وخالد والحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla rejects their theory: God's honoring is enabling piety and His abasement enabling sin, then the passage names their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: بل إكرامه العبد: تيسيره لتقواه، وإهانته: تيسيره للمعصية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says their worse failure is neglecting orphans and the poor, devouring inheritance like grazing animals, and hoarding wealth; a hadith praises a household that honors an orphan.
rows.anchor: وهو أن الله تعالى يكرمهم بكثرة المال، فلا يؤدون فيها ما يلزمهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readers use third-person verbs for honoring, encouraging, eating, and loving; the remaining canonical readers address the audience directly.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ومجاهد وأبو رجاء وقتادة والجحدري وأبو عمر: يكرمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, the Kufans, and Ibn Muqsim read taḥāḍḍūn with an open tāʾ and alif, from tataḥāḍḍūn: urging one another.
rows.anchor: وأبو جعفر وشيبة والكوفيون وابن مقسم: تحاضون بفتح التاء والألف

rows.speaker: عبد الله وعلقمة وزيد بن علي وابن المبارك والكسائي
rows.claim: These authorities read the same form with a damma on tāʾ, “you urge yourselves”; reciprocal and mutual verb forms can also mean a simple verb.
rows.anchor: وعبد الله أو علقمة وزيد بن علي وعبد الله بن المبارك والشيرزي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read the verbs actively, with “His punishment” and “His restraint” referring to God; no one else can carry out His punishment or restraint.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: لا يعذب، ولا يوثق: مبنيين للفاعل، والضمير في عذابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns may instead refer to the disbeliever punished by the guards; another view refers them to God but is weak because the verbs are future.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الضمير قبلها عائدا على الكافر، أي لا يعذب أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading group makes both verbs passive; the pronoun is most naturally attached to the object, so no one is punished or chained as severely as this person.
rows.anchor: بفتح الذال والثاء مبنيين للمفعول، فيجوز أن يكون الضمير فيهما مضافا للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive reading may mean no one bears another person's punishment, as in 6:164; grammarians dispute deriving a passive action from nouns such as ʿadhāb.
rows.anchor: أو يحمل أحد عذاب الإنسان لقوله تعالى: ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, and Nafiʿ have wiṯāq with kasra on waw; the majority use a fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع بخلاف عنهم: وثاقه بكسر الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punished one is generally any disbeliever; specific identifications include Umayya ibn Khalaf, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, or Iblis, though the following pronouns concern the human being.
rows.anchor: والمعذب هو الكافر على العموم. وقيل: هو أمية بن خلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tranquil soul is secure from fear and grief or settled in truth without doubt.
rows.anchor: الآمنة التي لا يلحقها خوف ولا حزن، أو التي كانت مطمئنة إلى الحق

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the address comes at death as the believer's soul leaves the body; others place it at resurrection or entry into Paradise.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: يقال لها ذلك عند الموت وخروجها من جسد المؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “To your Lord” can mean to His appointment; alternatively the Lord is the person rather than the soul, which is summoned back into bodies, and some take the address as a present exhortation to believers.
rows.anchor: إلى ربك: أي إلى موعد ربك. وقيل: الرب هنا الإنسان دون النفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul is pleased with what it receives and accepted by God; it is told to join the company of righteous servants and enter Paradise with them.
rows.anchor: راضية بما أوتيته، مرضية عند الله. فادخلي في عبادي: أي في جملة عبادي الصالحين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the soul as spirit and “enter among My servants” as entering the servants' bodies.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النفس والروح، والمعنى: فادخلي في أجساد عبادي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة والضحاك ومجاهد وأبو جعفر وأبو صالح والكلبي
rows.claim: Most readers use the plural “My servants”; these authorities read the singular “My servant.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: في عبادي جمعا وابن عباس وعكرمة والضحاك ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular can be a generic noun with the same denotation as the plural; alternatively it means entering the servant's body.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أنه أريد به اسم الجنس، فمدلوله ومدلول الجمع واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first “enter” takes fī because the destination is not a literal container, while the second normally takes no preposition because Paradise is a real place entered.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنه إذا كان المدخول فيه غير ظرف حقيقي تعددت إليه بفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse has also been specifically associated with ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, Hamza, or Khubayb ibn ʿAdi.
rows.anchor: قيل: في عثمان بن عفان. وقيل: في حمزة. وقيل: في خبيب بن عدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabad means hardship, extended from pain and swelling of the liver to all toil and difficulty; Labid and Abu al-Asbaʿ give poetic examples.
rows.anchor: الكبد: الشدة والمشقة، وأصله من كبد الرجل كبدا فهو أكبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for lip is originally shafahah with its hāʾ deleted, supported by diminutive, plural, and verb forms; despite feminine tāʾ, it does not take the regular feminine plural.
rows.anchor: الشفة معروفة، وأصلها شفهة، حذفت منها الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najd is a high neck or path; the region Najd is named for rising above low-lying Tihama, and a verse by Imruʾ al-Qays illustrates the term.
rows.anchor: النجد: العنق وجمعه نجود، وبه سميت نجد لارتفاعها عن انخفاض تهامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fakk means freeing one thing from another; a poet uses it of releasing a captive from a shackle.
rows.anchor: الفك: تخليص الشيء من الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saghab is widespread hunger; a person is said to saghiba when hungry.
rows.anchor: السغب: الجوع العام، وقد يقال سغب الرجل إذا جاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tariba means becoming poor and lying in the dirt; atraba means becoming wealthy, like having earth in abundance, and is related to athra.
rows.anchor: ترب الرجل، إذا افتقر ولصق بالتراب، وأترب، إذا استغنى وصار ذا مال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awsada and aṣada both mean to shut and close a door; a poem describes closed gates.
rows.anchor: أوصدت الباب وآصدته، إذا أغلقته وأطبقته

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most authorities call the surah Meccan; another view says it is Medinan.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية في قول الجمهور، وقيل: مدنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah follows the preceding account of prosperity, restricted provision, bad traits, and afterlife outcomes with another test of human conduct.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى ابتلاءه للإنسان بحالة التنعيم وحالة التقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The city named in the oath is Mecca.
rows.anchor: والإشارة لهذا البلد إلى مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers the circumstantial sense “you are residing here,” honoring the city through the Prophet's presence alongside its sanctity and its attribution to God.
rows.anchor: وأنت حل: جملة حالية تفيد تعظيم المقسم به، أي فأنت مقيم به

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وجماعة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas and others read “you are lawful here,” meaning the Prophet could kill whom he wished on the day of Mecca's conquest; Ibn ʿAṭiyya ties this to taking lā as negation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وجماعة: معناه: وأنت حلال بهذا البلد، يحل لك فيه قتل من شئت

rows.speaker: شرحبيل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sharhabil ibn Saʿd says the people made the Prophet lawful to abuse, kill, and expel; al-Zamakhshari uses this to console him and explain the oath, and also proposes future permission at the conquest.
rows.anchor: وقال شرحبيل بن سعد: يعني وأنت حل بهذا البلد، جعلوك حلالا مستحل الأذى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari argues that “you are lawful” refers to a future conquest, supporting the future use of the participle with 39:30.
rows.anchor: إن السورة بالاتفاق مكية، وأين الهجرة من وقت نزولها؟ فما بال الفتح؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the future-only argument: a circumstantial participle can describe the present, and the verse does not say the Prophet was permitted to kill at revelation; the surah's Meccan status is disputed.
rows.anchor: وحمله على أن الجملة اعتراضية لا يتعين، وقد ذكرنا أولا أنها جملة حالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense is that the Prophet resided in Mecca when revealed; the verse does not imply its people considered him lawful or that he was then permitted to capture or kill.
rows.anchor: بل الظاهر ما ذكرناه أولا من أنه تعالى أقسم بها لما جمعت من الشرفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A father and what he begot” is generic rather than a specific individual; Ibn ʿAbbas includes all parents and offspring among animals, and Mujahid says Adam and his descendants.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: ووالد وما ولد، لا يراد به معين، بل ينطلق على كل والد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views identify the pair as righteous descendants, Noah and his offspring, Abraham and his offspring, or the Prophet's father and Abraham's descendants.
rows.anchor: وقيل: والصالحين من ذريته. وقيل: نوح وذريته

rows.speaker: الطبري والماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi suggest the father is the Prophet and what he begot is his community, citing his saying he is like a father to them and the wording about his wives as their mothers.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري والماوردي: يحتمل أن يكون الوالد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari identifies the father and offspring as the Prophet and his descendants; the indefinite wording conveys praise and wonder at their remarkable nature.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: ما المراد بوالد وما ولد؟ قلت: رسول الله

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says mā can refer to people, as in “whatever is lawful to you” and “what created male and female,” where God is the creator.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: وصلح ما للناس، كقوله: ما طاب لكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة وابن جبير
rows.claim: They take wālid as a begetting man and mā as a barren woman who did not give birth; the required omitted relative pronoun is unacceptable to Basran grammarians.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وعكرمة وابن جبير: المراد بالوالد الذي يولد له

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most take al-insan generically and fi kabad as enduring the innumerable hardships of worldly and afterlife life, ending in relief in Paradise or multiplied hardship in Hell.
rows.anchor: والجمهور: على أن الإنسان اسم جنس، وفي كبد: يكابد مشاق الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعبد الله بن شداد وأبو صالح والضحاك ومجاهد
rows.claim: These authorities explain fi kabad as standing upright rather than lying face down, a blessing granted to humanity.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وعبد الله بن شداد وأبو صالح والضحاك ومجاهد: في كبد معناه

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan says the human is upright-headed in the womb, then turns head-down when permitted to emerge.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن كيسان: منتصبا رأسه في بطن أمه

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says the human struggles to give thanks in prosperity and to be patient in adversity.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عمر: يكابد الشكر على السراء، ويكابد الصبر على الضراء

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the human is Adam and kabad means the sky; Abu Hayyan calls such alternatives weak and prefers the general hardship sense.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: الإنسان: آدم، في كبد: في السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human presumes his strength makes him unchallengeable, boasts of spending a great fortune for praise, and assumes no one sees his motives; recording angels preserve his deeds for Judgment.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الضمير في أيحسب عائد على الإنسان، أي هو لشدة شكيمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other identifications include Quraysh leaders, Abu al-Asad Asid ibn Kulda, who boasted no one could move him from a hide, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو أبو الأسد أسيد بن كلدة، كان يبسط له الأديم العكاظي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Harith ibn ʿAmir ibn Nawfal complained that following Muhammad had cost him much money through expiations and liabilities prescribed after sins.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحرث بن عامر بن نوفل، وكان إذا أذنب استفتى النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary the vowels and doubling in lubadan: most use a damma then fatḥa, Abu Jaʿfar doubles bāʾ, he and Zayd ibn ʿAli also have a still bāʾ, and Mujahid and Ibn Abi al-Zinad use two dammas.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: لبدا، بضم اللام وفتح الباء وأبو جعفر: بشد الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two eyes let a person see; the tongue expresses what is inside, while the lips close the mouth and aid eating, drinking, and blowing.
rows.anchor: ألم نجعل له عينين يبصر بهما، ولسانا يفصح عما في باطنه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس والجمهور
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, and most authorities interpret the two high paths as the paths of good and evil.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود وابن عباس والجمهور: طريق الخير والشر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعلي وابن المسيب والضحاك
rows.claim: Another view from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAli, Ibn al-Musayyib, and al-Dahhak identifies the two paths as the two breasts that nourish a child.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا، وعلي وابن المسيب والضحاك: الثديين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Failing to climb the obstacle means failing to thank God for the preceding gifts; the difficult charitable work is like ascending a steep pass, and iqtiham means entering with force and speed.
rows.anchor: فلا اقتحم العقبة: أي لم يشكر تلك النعم السابقة، والعقبة استعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtiham also means throwing oneself into something without deliberation; a severe year is called a qahmah, and the verb describes rushing into a matter.
rows.anchor: رمى نفسه فيه من غير روية. والظاهر أن لا للنفي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: They take lā as negation: despite being given faculties and guidance, the person did no good; the following faith clause can supply the usual repeated lā, as in 92:15.
rows.anchor: وهو قول أبي عبيدة والفراء والزجاج، كأنه قال: وهبنا له الجوارح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations take the phrase as a curse that he may do no good, or as exhortation; Abu Hayyan says lā alone is not known to express exhortation without hamza.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو جار مجرى الدعاء، كقوله: لا نجا ولا سلم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the obstacle is Hell, from which only these good deeds can deliver a person.
rows.anchor: وقيل: العقبة: جهنم، لا ينجي منها إلا هذه الأعمال، قاله الحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وكعب
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Kaʿb say the obstacle is a mountain in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ومجاهد وكعب: جبل في جهنم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats lā as repeated semantically: failing to climb means failing to free a slave or feed a poor person; Abu Hayyan says this depends on reading fakk as a past verb.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري، بعد أن تنحل مقالة الفراء والزجاج: هي بمعنى لا متكررة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and two grammarians read fakk and aṭʿama as past verbs, with raqabah accusative; the other canonical readers make fakk a nominative verbal noun and coordinate the genitive iṭʿām.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير والنحويان: فك فعلا ماضيا، رقبة نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAli and Abu Raja follow Ibn Kathir but read dhā masghabah with alif; al-Hasan and Abu Raja also read dhā as an object meaning a hungry person, with the orphan dependent on it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي وأبو رجاء كقراءة ابن كثير، إلا أنهما قرآ: ذا مسغبة بالألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Followers annex fakk to raqabah and use aṭʿama as a past verb; the verbal-noun reading explains the obstacle, while past verbs need no omitted annexed noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض التابعين: فك رقبة بالإضافة، أو أطعم فعلا ماضيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Freeing the neck means releasing a person from captivity and bondage; a near relative combines charity with maintaining kinship ties.
rows.anchor: وفك الرقبة: تخليصها من الأسر والرق. ذا مقربة: ليجتمع صدقة وصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw marks types of charitable deed, and describing the day as one of hunger is broad usage; the destitute person lies on the road in dust without a home.
rows.anchor: وأو هنا للتنويع، ووصف يوم بذي مسغبة على الاتساع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas defines a person of dust as one who leaves home and turns back, certain that only dirt remains there.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هو الذي يخرج من بيته، ثم يقلب وجهه إليه مستيقنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about becoming one of the believers is coordinated with the failure to climb; thumma marks rank or order of mention, not time, since belief must precede good deeds and persist until death for them to benefit.
rows.anchor: ثم كان من الذين آمنوا: هذا معطوف على قوله: فلا اقتحم ودخلت ثم لتراخي الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutual exhortation to patience means steadfastness in faith and obedience and abstention from sins; exhortation to mercy means compassion or acts that bring God's mercy.
rows.anchor: وتواصوا بالصبر: أي أوصى بعضهم بعضا بالصبر على الإيمان والطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meanings of the people of the right and left were discussed in Surat al-Waqiʿah.
rows.anchor: والميمنة والمشأمة تقدم القول فيهما في الواقعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, and Hafs use a hamza in muʾṣadah here and in al-Humazah; other canonical readers omit it, with both forms explained from verbs for closing. A poem uses the hamzated form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وحمزة وحفص: مؤصدة بالهمز هنا وفي الهمزة
